questions.stem:
Two tunnels are planned to be dug through Sydney’s Blue Mountains to improve traffic infrastructure.

Digging at one end of the tunnel is to begin at the point \((-9,\ 15,\ 7)\) at Blackheath and continue in the direction \(7\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}\). The digging at the other end of the tunnel will start at the coordinate \((33,\ 5,\ -1)\) near Springwood and continue in the direction \(-14\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{k}\). Both sections are to be straight lines.

The coordinates are measured relative to a fixed origin \(O\), where one unit is 500 metres.

meta.source: Abbotsleigh 2021 4U Trials & Solutions

parts.stem: Show that the two sections of the tunnel will eventually meet at a point near Wentworth Falls and find the coordinates of this point.
parts.hint: Equate the components of the two vector equations; solve j and k first, then check i.

steps.explain: Write a vector equation for each section.
If they meet, all three components are equal for some \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\).
Solve the two simple equations first.
Check the \(\mathbf{i}\) equation with these values. It is satisfied, so the lines really do meet.
Substitute \(\lambda=2\) to get the meeting point.

parts.stem: Show that the points \(L(-5,6,-5)\), \(M(7,-2,-1)\) and \(N(10,-4,0)\) are collinear.
parts.hint: Show LM is a multiple of MN.

steps.explain: Find \(\overrightarrow{LM}\).
Find \(\overrightarrow{MN}\).
Compare.
The vectors are parallel and share the point \(M\), so \(L\), \(M\), \(N\) lie on one line.

meta.source: Blacktown Boys 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

parts.answer: \(\overrightarrow{LM}=12\mathbf{i}-8\mathbf{j}+4\mathbf{k}=4(3\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})\), \(\overrightarrow{MN}=3\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}\). So LM = 4MN: parallel with common point M, hence collinear.

keyPoints.note: Parallel vectors with a common point are on one line.

parts.stem: Hence find the ratio in which \(M\) divides \(LN\).
parts.hint: Use LM = 4MN.

steps.explain: From (i), \(\overrightarrow{LM}=4\overrightarrow{MN}\): \(LM\) is 4 times as long as \(MN\), in the same direction.
So \(M\) divides \(LN\) internally in the ratio \(4:1\).

meta.source: Blacktown Boys 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

keyPoints.note: The ratio is LM : MN.

meta.source: Blacktown Boys 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

parts.stem: Determine the equation of the line vector \(\mathbf{r}\), given that it passes through the point \((-3,5,-1)\) and is parallel to the line joining \(P(3,1,-1)\) and \(Q(5,0,2)\).
parts.hint: Point (−3, 5, −1) + λ × PQ.

steps.explain: Direction: parallel to \(PQ\).
Line through \((-3,5,-1)\) with that direction.

meta.source: Blacktown Boys 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

keyPoints.note: Direction vector = Q − P; position vector = the given point.

parts.stem: Show that the point \((7,0,14)\) lies on this line.
parts.hint: Find λ from one component and check the others.

steps.explain: Find \(\lambda\) from the first component.
Check the other components with \(\lambda=5\).
One value of \(\lambda\) gives all three coordinates, so the point is on the line.

meta.source: Blacktown Boys 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

parts.answer: First component: −3 + 2λ = 7 ⇒ λ = 5. Then y = 5 − 5 = 0 ✓, z = −1 + 15 = 14 ✓. So (7, 0, 14) is on the line.

keyPoints.note: One λ must work for all three components.

questions.stem: A line passes through the points \(A(1,-1,3)\) and \(B(0,5,8)\). Find the midpoint of the segment \(AB\).
questions.hint: The midpoint is the point halfway along the segment: \(\lambda = 0.5\) in \(\underset{\sim}{r}=\underset{\sim}{a}+\lambda\underset{\sim}{b}\).

steps.explain: Use the vector equation from part (i): \(\underset{\sim}{r}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\ 3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 6\\ 5\end{pmatrix}\).
The midpoint is halfway along AB, so \(\lambda = 0.5\).
Substitute \(\lambda = 0.5\): \(\underset{\sim}{r}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\ 3\end{pmatrix}+0.5\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 6\\ 5\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0.5\\ 2\\ 5.5\end{pmatrix}\).
Check: the midpoint is the average of A and B: \(\dfrac{1+0}{2}=0.5\), \(\dfrac{-1+5}{2}=2\), \(\dfrac{3+8}{2}=5.5\). Answer: \(M(0.5,2,5.5)\).

keyPoints.note: The midpoint has \(\lambda = 0.5\).

meta.source: Cheltenham Girls High School 2023 HSC Trial Assessment Task 4 (Mathematics Extension 2)

questions.stem: Hence, find the point \(P\) which divides the segment \(AB\) internally in the ratio \(3:2\).
questions.hint: For internal division in the ratio \(m:n\), \(\lambda = \dfrac{m}{m+n}\). Here \(m=3\) and \(n=2\).

steps.explain: Identify the ratio. P divides AB internally in the ratio 3:2, so the part from A to P is 3 parts and the whole segment is 5 parts.
Substitute \(\lambda = \dfrac35\) into the line equation.
Check: \(\lambda = 0.5\) gave the midpoint, and \(\lambda=0.6\) should be closer to B (which is at \(\lambda = 1\)). The point \((0.4, 2.6, 6)\) is 60% of the way from A to B.

keyPoints.note: Use \(\lambda=\dfrac{m}{m+n}=\dfrac{3}{5}\).

meta.source: Cheltenham Girls High School 2023 HSC Trial Assessment Task 4 (Mathematics Extension 2)

questions.stem: A line passes through the points \(A(1,-1,3)\) and \(B(0,5,8)\). Show that the vector equation of the line is \(\underset{\sim}{r}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\ 3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 6\\ 5\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: Direction \(\vec{AB}=B-A=(-1,6,5)\). Use A as the position vector \(\underset{\sim}{a}\). Then \(\underset{\sim}{r}=\underset{\sim}{a}+\lambda\vec{AB}\).
questions.hint: Find the direction vector \(\vec{AB}\) first, then use A as the point on the line.

steps.explain: Direction vector: \(\vec{AB}=\underset{\sim}{b}-\underset{\sim}{a}=(0,5,8)-(1,-1,3)=(-1,6,5)\).
A point on the line is A itself, with position vector \((1,-1,3)\).
Combine: \(\underset{\sim}{r}=\underset{\sim}{a}+\lambda\vec{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\ 3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 6\\ 5\end{pmatrix}\). Shown.

meta.source: Cheltenham Girls High School 2023 HSC Trial Assessment Task 4 (Mathematics Extension 2)

questions.stem: A line passes through the points \(A(1,3,-2)\) and \(B(2,-1,5)\). Show that the vector equation of the line \(AB\) is given by \(\mathbf{r}=(\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k})+\lambda_1(\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j}+7\mathbf{k}),\ \lambda_1\in\mathbb{R}\).
questions.answer: Position vector of \(A\): \(\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k}\). Direction \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}=(2-1)\mathbf{i}+(-1-3)\mathbf{j}+(5+2)\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j}+7\mathbf{k}\). So \(\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{a}+\lambda\overrightarrow{AB}\) is the required equation. ∎
questions.hint: A line needs a POINT on it and a DIRECTION: use \(A\) as the point and \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) as the direction.

steps.explain: Position vector of the point \(A\).
Direction vector: end minus start.
Simplify.
Vector equation of a line: point plus a multiple of the direction.

keyPoints.note: Point A plus a multiple of the vector AB.

meta.source: Cranbrook School 2020 Mathematics Extension 2 HSC Trial Examination (Assessment Task 3)

questions.hint: The point is on the line only if ONE value of \(\lambda_1\) gives ALL THREE coordinates. Find \(\lambda_1\) from one coordinate, then test the other two.

steps.explain: Write the coordinates of a general point on the line.
Match \(x=3\).
Test this in the \(y\) and \(z\) equations.
The value does not give \(C\)'s coordinates, so \(C\) is NOT on the line.

keyPoints.note: One value of the parameter must fit all three coordinates.

questions.hint: Section formula: a point dividing \(AC\) in the ratio \(m:n\) is \(\dfrac{n\,A+m\,C}{m+n}\). Apply it to each coordinate separately.

steps.explain: Let \(A=(-1,0,3)\), \(B=(3,a,5)\), \(C=(5,3,b)\). \(B\) is two parts from \(A\) and one part from \(C\), so \(AB:BC=2:1\) and \(B=\dfrac{1\cdot A+2\cdot C}{3}\).

questions.stem: Using vectors, determine whether the points \(A(0,4,4)\), \(B(8,20,36)\) and \(C(12,28,52)\) are collinear.
questions.hint: Three points are collinear exactly when \(\overrightarrow{AC}\) is a SCALAR MULTIPLE of \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) (parallel vectors sharing the point \(A\)). Compute both vectors as (end \(-\) start) and compare their components.

steps.explain: Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}=B-A\) (end minus start), component by component.
Find \(\overrightarrow{AC}=C-A\).
Compare the components: each component of \(\overrightarrow{AC}\) divided by the matching component of \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) must give the SAME number \(k\).
All three ratios equal \(\dfrac{3}{2}\), so \(\overrightarrow{AC}=\dfrac{3}{2}\overrightarrow{AB}\): the vectors are parallel AND share the point \(A\), so \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) lie on one line.
Why not the others: B only says the vectors are not EQUAL (they only need to be parallel); C compares lengths (collinear points can be at any distances); D uses wrong vector components.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Collinear \(\Leftrightarrow\overrightarrow{AC}=k\overrightarrow{AB}\).

questions.stem: A line passes through the points \(A(-3,2,6)\) and \(B(7,4,-3)\). Determine if \(C(-13,0,15)\) lies on the line.
options: \(\begin{aligned}&-13=-3+10\lambda\Rightarrow\lambda=-1;\quad0=2+2\lambda\Rightarrow\lambda=-1;\quad15=6-9\lambda\Rightarrow\lambda=-1\\ &\text{same }\lambda\text{ in all three}\Rightarrow C\text{ lies on the line}\end{aligned}\)

\(\begin{aligned}&-13=-3+10\lambda\Rightarrow\lambda=-1;\quad0=2+2\lambda\Rightarrow\lambda=-1;\quad15=6-9\lambda\Rightarrow\lambda=1\\ &\lambda\text{ values differ}\Rightarrow C\text{ is not on the line}\end{aligned}\)

\(\begin{aligned}&-13=-3+10\lambda\Rightarrow\lambda=1;\quad0=2+2\lambda\Rightarrow\lambda=-1;\quad15=6-9\lambda\Rightarrow\lambda=-1\\ &\lambda\text{ values differ}\Rightarrow C\text{ is not on the line}\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}&-13=-3+10\lambda\Rightarrow\lambda=-1\\ &\text{only one coordinate is needed}\Rightarrow C\text{ is not on the line}\end{aligned}\)
questions.hint: Put the coordinates of \(C\) into the parametric equations \(x=-3+10\lambda\), \(y=2+2\lambda\), \(z=6-9\lambda\). \(C\) is on the line only if ONE value of \(\lambda\) works for ALL THREE equations.

steps.explain: Use the parametric equations from part (ii) and substitute \(C(-13,0,15)\) into each.
\(x\): \(-13=-3+10\lambda\Rightarrow10\lambda=-10\Rightarrow\lambda=-1\).
\(y\): \(0=2+2\lambda\Rightarrow2\lambda=-2\Rightarrow\lambda=-1\).
\(z\): \(15=6-9\lambda\Rightarrow-9\lambda=9\Rightarrow\lambda=-1\).
The SAME \(\lambda=-1\) satisfies all three equations, so \(C\) is the point on the line reached at \(\lambda=-1\) (one step BEFORE \(A\)). Hence \(C\) lies on the line.

questions.stem: Consider the line \(\underset{\sim}{r}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\ 3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-5\\ 3\end{pmatrix}\) where \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\). Show that the point \((0,6)\) lies on \(\underset{\sim}{r}\).
options: \(\begin{aligned}&5-5\lambda=0\Rightarrow\lambda=1;\quad3+3\lambda=6\Rightarrow\lambda=1\\ &\text{the same }\lambda=1\text{ works for both, so }(0,6)\text{ lies on }\underset{\sim}{r}\end{aligned}\)
questions.hint: A point is on the line if there is ONE value of \(\lambda\) that gives BOTH its coordinates. Write \(x=5-5\lambda\), \(y=3+3\lambda\) and solve each for \(\lambda\) using \(x=0\), \(y=6\).

steps.explain: Write the line as two equations, one per component.
Put \(x=0\): \(0=5-5\lambda\Rightarrow5\lambda=5\Rightarrow\lambda=1\).
Put \(y=6\): \(6=3+3\lambda\Rightarrow3\lambda=3\Rightarrow\lambda=1\).

Both coordinates give the SAME \(\lambda=1\), so \((0,6)\) is the point of the line at \(\lambda=1\). Check: \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\ 3\end{pmatrix}+1\begin{pmatrix}-5\\ 3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 6\end{pmatrix}\) ✓. ∎
Why not the others: B, C and D contain an arithmetic slip, so they produce two different \(\lambda\) values and wrongly conclude the point is not on the line.
So the correct choice is option A.

meta.source: Baulkham Hills 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

parts.stem: Explain why these lines are not parallel.
parts.hint: Parallel ⇔ direction vectors are scalar multiples.

steps.explain: Lines are parallel exactly when their direction vectors are multiples of each other.
If \((4,-11,3)=k(1,4,1)\) then \(k=4\) from the first component, but \(4\times4=16\neq-11\). No such \(k\).
So the lines are not parallel. (Different position vectors or lengths don't decide it; a non-zero dot product only shows they aren't perpendicular.)

meta.source: Baulkham Hills 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

options: Their direction vectors have different lengths.
The dot product of the direction vectors is not zero.
The direction vectors \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 4\\ 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\ -11\\ 3\end{pmatrix}\) are not scalar multiples of each other.

keyPoints.note: Check whether (4, −11, 3) is a multiple of (1, 4, 1).

parts.stem: Determine whether these lines are skew or whether they intersect.
parts.hint: Solve two component equations for λ and μ, then test the third.

steps.explain: Equate the components.
From the first and third: \(\lambda-4\mu=-6\) and \(\lambda-3\mu=-3\). Subtract.
Check the second equation.
No common point, and from (i) they are not parallel, so the lines are skew.

meta.source: Baulkham Hills 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

options: They are parallel, so they never meet.
They are skew: the values from two component equations do not satisfy the third.

keyPoints.note: Find λ, μ from two components; if the third fails, the lines are skew.

questions.stem: A line passes through the points \(A(1,3,-2)\) and \(B(2,-1,5)\). Consider a line with parametric equations \(x=1-\lambda_2,\ y=2+3\lambda_2\) and \(z=-1+\lambda_2\). Assuming the line is neither parallel or perpendicular to \(AB\), determine whether the lines intersect or are skew.
options: Skew: no values of \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) satisfy all three equations.
questions.hint: Set the two lines equal. Use TWO of the three coordinate equations to find \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\), then CHECK those values in the third. If the third fails, the lines are skew.

steps.explain: Equate the coordinates (line 1: \((1+\lambda_1,\ 3-4\lambda_1,\ -2+7\lambda_1)\)).
From the first equation.
Substitute into the second.
Test in the THIRD equation.
No values satisfy all three equations, so the lines never meet. They are not parallel (assumed), so they are SKEW.

keyPoints.note: Solve two equations, test the third.

questions.stem: Find the point of intersection of the lines \(\underset{\sim}{r}=(1,7,5)+\lambda(1,-2,2)\) and \(\underset{\sim}{r}=(2,1,3)+\mu(0,1,1)\).
questions.hint: Set the coordinates equal: three equations in \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\). Solve two, check the third.

steps.explain: Equate the components.
From the first: \(\lambda=1\). Then the second gives \(7-2=5=1+\mu\Rightarrow\mu=4\).
Check the third: \(5+2=7=3+4\) ✓ (consistent: the lines do meet).
Substitute \(\lambda=1\) into the first line.

keyPoints.note: Equate coordinates; solve two equations and check the third.

questions.stem: Show that the line \(\begin{pmatrix}-8\\ 12\\ 2\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}6\\-8\\ 5\end{pmatrix}\) is skew to the line \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\-6\\ 6\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 3\\-4\end{pmatrix}\). Which statement correctly shows the lines are skew?
options: The direction vectors are parallel, so the lines are skew
Solving two equations gives \(\lambda_{1}=-2\), \(\lambda_{2}=3\), which also satisfy the third, so the lines meet
The direction vectors are not parallel, and solving two of the equations gives \(\lambda_{1}=-2\), \(\lambda_{2}=3\), which fail the third (\(4(-2)+5(3)=7\ne4\)), so they never meet
The direction vectors are not parallel, so the lines must intersect
questions.hint: Skew lines are NOT parallel and do NOT intersect. Equate the two lines, solve two equations, and test the answer in the third.

steps.explain: Check the direction vectors: \((1,3,-4)\) and \((6,-8,5)\). Neither is a multiple of the other, so the lines are NOT parallel.
Look for an intersection: equate the lines (use \(\lambda_{1}\) and \(\lambda_{2}\) for the two parameters), giving three equations.
Solve (1) and (2): from (1) \(\lambda_{1}=6\lambda_{2}-20\), so \(3(6\lambda_{2}-20)+8\lambda_{2}=18\), giving \(26\lambda_{2}=78\).
Test in equation (3): \(4(-2)+5(3)=-8+15=7\), but the right side is 4. The values do not satisfy (3), so there is NO common point.
The lines are not parallel and do not intersect: they are skew.
So the correct choice is option C.

keyPoints.note: Skew means not parallel and never meeting: solve two equations, test the third.

questions.stem: Vectors \(\underset{\sim}{u}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{v}\) have components \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 3\\ 2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\ t\\ 4\end{pmatrix}\) respectively. The following statements are made about \(\underset{\sim}{u}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{v}\): Statement I: When \(t=5\), \(\underset{\sim}{u}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{v}\) are parallel. Statement II: When \(t=\dfrac{1}{5}\), \(\underset{\sim}{v}\) is a unit vector. Which of the following is true?
questions.hint: Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other: all three component ratios must be equal. A unit vector has magnitude 1.

steps.explain: Statement I: for \(\underset{\sim}{v}=\lambda\underset{\sim}{u}\) the ratios of matching components must all be equal. With \(t=5\):
The ratios \(3,\ \dfrac{5}{3},\ 2\) are not equal, so \(\underset{\sim}{u}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{v}\) are NOT parallel. Statement I is false.
Statement II: magnitude of \(\underset{\sim}{v}\) with \(t=\dfrac{1}{5}\).
\(\sqrt{\dfrac{626}{25}}\approx5.003\ne1\), so \(\underset{\sim}{v}\) is NOT a unit vector. Statement II is false.
Both statements are incorrect.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Which of the following is true
keyPoints.note: Parallel means all component ratios equal; unit means magnitude 1.

questions.stem: Two lines, \(l_{1}\) and \(l_{2}\), are given below. \(l_{1}:\ \underset{\sim}{r}(t)=2\underset{\sim}{i}+3\underset{\sim}{k}+t\left(\underset{\sim}{i}-\underset{\sim}{j}+2\underset{\sim}{k}\right)\), \(\ l_{2}:\ \dfrac{x-2}{2}=\dfrac{y+1}{-1}=\dfrac{z-4}{3}\). Show that \(l_{1}\) and \(l_{2}\) intersect. Which working is correct?
options: \(l_{1}:(x,y,z)=(2+t,\,-t,\,3+2t)\); \(l_{2}:(x,y,z)=(2+2\lambda,\,-1-\lambda,\,4+3\lambda)\). Equate \(x,y\): \(t=2\lambda\) and \(-t=-1-\lambda\) give \(\lambda=1,\ t=2\). Check \(z\): \(3+2(2)=7\) and \(4+3(1)=7\) ✓. Same point \((4,-2,7)\), so the lines intersect.

\(l_{1}:(2+t,\,-t,\,3+2t)\); \(l_{2}:(2+2\lambda,\,-1-\lambda,\,4+3\lambda)\). Equate \(x,y\): \(t=2\lambda\) and \(-t=-1-\lambda\) give \(\lambda=1,\ t=2\). Check \(z\): \(3+2(2)=7\) but \(4+3(1)=6\), so the lines do not intersect.
The direction vectors are \((1,-1,2)\) and \((2,-1,3)\). They are not parallel, so the lines must intersect.
Equate only \(x\) and \(y\): \(t=2\lambda\) and \(-t=-1-\lambda\) give \(\lambda=1,\ t=2\). Two equations are satisfied, so the lines intersect (no need to check \(z\)).
questions.hint: Write both lines in parametric form with DIFFERENT parameters (\(t\) and \(\lambda\)). Equate any two coordinates to find \(t,\lambda\), then CHECK the third coordinate.

steps.explain: Convert both lines to parametric form. \(l_{1}\): \(x=2+t,\ y=-t,\ z=3+2t\). \(l_{2}\): set each fraction equal to \(\lambda\): \(x=2+2\lambda,\ y=-1-\lambda,\ z=4+3\lambda\).
If the lines meet, a common point has equal coordinates. Equate \(x\) and \(y\).
Solve (1) and (2): \(2\lambda=1+\lambda\), so \(\lambda=1\) and \(t=2\).
Check the THIRD coordinate (the lines are 3D and may be skew): \(l_{1}\): \(3+2(2)=7\). \(l_{2}\): \(4+3(1)=7\). Equal ✓.
Both lines pass through \((4,-2,7)\), so \(l_{1}\) and \(l_{2}\) intersect.
Why not the others: B has an arithmetic slip (\(4+3=7\), not 6); C ignores the possibility that lines in 3D can be skew (not parallel and not intersecting); D skips the check of the third equation.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Equate two coordinates to find t and lambda, then check the third.

questions.stem: Two lines, \(l_{1}\) and \(l_{2}\), have direction vectors \(\underset{\sim}{b}_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}\) (from \(l_{1}:\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=2\underset{\sim}{i}+3\underset{\sim}{k}+t\left(\underset{\sim}{i}-\underset{\sim}{j}+2\underset{\sim}{k}\right)\)) and \(\underset{\sim}{b}_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\ 3\end{pmatrix}\) (from \(l_{2}:\dfrac{x-2}{2}=\dfrac{y+1}{-1}=\dfrac{z-4}{3}\)). Find the acute angle between \(l_{1}\) and \(l_{2}\), to the nearest minute.
questions.hint: The angle between two lines is the angle between their direction vectors: \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{\underset{\sim}{b}_{1}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}_{2}}{|\underset{\sim}{b}_{1}||\underset{\sim}{b}_{2}|}\). Use the positive value for the acute angle.

steps.explain: Dot product (multiply matching components and add).
Magnitudes.
Substitute: \(\sqrt{6}\times\sqrt{14}=\sqrt{84}=9.165\).
Inverse cosine, then convert the decimal part to minutes: \(0.894^{\circ}\times60=53.6'\approx54'\).
The dot product is positive, so the angle is already acute. Option B is \(90^{\circ}-\theta\); option C divides by \(6\times14\) instead of \(\sqrt{6}\sqrt{14}\); option D is \(180^{\circ}-\theta\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: cos theta equals dot product over product of magnitudes.

questions.stem: With respect to a fixed origin \(O\), the lines \(l_{1}\) and \(l_{2}\) are given by \(l_{1}:\ \mathbf{r}=9\mathbf{i}+13\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k}+\lambda(\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k})\) and \(l_{2}:\ \mathbf{r}=2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}+\mu(2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})\), where \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) are scalar parameters. Given that \(l_{1}\) and \(l_{2}\) meet, find the position vector of their point of intersection.
questions.hint: At the intersection both lines give the SAME point: set the \(\mathbf{i}\), \(\mathbf{j}\), \(\mathbf{k}\) components equal. Use two equations to find \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\), check the third, then substitute back.

steps.explain: Write both lines in components. \(l_{1}\): \((9+\lambda,\ 13+4\lambda,\ -3-2\lambda)\). \(l_{2}\): \((2+2\mu,\ -1+\mu,\ 1+\mu)\).
From the \(\mathbf{i}\) equation: \(\lambda=2\mu-7\). (\(\dagger\))
Substitute into the \(\mathbf{j}\) equation \(13+4\lambda=-1+\mu\).
Check with the \(\mathbf{k}\) equation: \(-3-2(-3)=3\) and \(1+\mu=3\) ✓ (so the lines really meet).
Substitute \(\lambda=-3\) into \(l_{1}\) (or \(\mu=2\) into \(l_{2}\)).

Why not the others: \(9\mathbf{i}+13\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k}\) is the point of \(l_{1}\) with \(\lambda=0\), \(2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}\) is the point with \(\mu=0\); the last option has a wrong \(\mathbf{k}\)-component.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: find the position vector of their point of intersection
keyPoints.note: Equate components; check the third equation.

questions.stem: With respect to a fixed origin \(O\), the lines \(l_{1}\) and \(l_{2}\) are given by \(l_{1}:\ \mathbf{r}=9\mathbf{i}+13\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k}+\lambda(\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k})\) and \(l_{2}:\ \mathbf{r}=2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}+\mu(2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})\), where \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) are scalar parameters. Find the acute angle between \(l_{1}\) and \(l_{2}\), correct to the nearest tenth of a degree.
questions.hint: The angle between two lines is the angle between their DIRECTION vectors (the vectors multiplying \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\)). Use \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}}{|\underset{\sim}{a}||\underset{\sim}{b}|}\). If it is obtuse, take the acute angle.

steps.explain: Direction vectors: \(\underset{\sim}{a}=(1,4,-2)\) for \(l_{1}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{b}=(2,1,1)\) for \(l_{2}\).
Dot product.
Lengths.
Angle formula.
Inverse cosine (degree mode). The cosine is POSITIVE, so \(\theta\) is already acute.
Why not the others: \(110.9^{\circ}=180^{\circ}-69.1^{\circ}\) is the obtuse angle (not asked); \(20.9^{\circ}=90^{\circ}-69.1^{\circ}\); \(54.7^{\circ}\) comes from a wrong length.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Find the point of intersection of \(\underset{\sim}{r_{1}}=\begin{bmatrix}4\\ 8\\ 3\end{bmatrix}+\lambda\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 2\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{r_{2}}=\begin{bmatrix}9\\ 6\\ 10\end{bmatrix}+\mu\begin{bmatrix}1\\-4\\ 2\end{bmatrix}\).
questions.hint: At the intersection BOTH lines give the SAME point: equate the \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) components (3 equations, 2 unknowns \(\lambda,\mu\)). Solve two equations, then CHECK in the third.

steps.explain: Equate components.
From the first: \(\lambda=5+\mu\). Substitute into the third: \(3+5+\mu=10+2\mu\Rightarrow\mu=-2\), so \(\lambda=3\).
Check in the second: \(8+2(3)=14\) and \(6-4(-2)=14\) ✓ (all three equations agree: the lines intersect).
Point of intersection: put \(\lambda=3\) into \(r_{1}\) (or \(\mu=-2\) into \(r_{2}\)).
Why not the others: B and C are the starting points of the lines; D would be true only if the second check failed.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: The line \(l_{2}\) has the vector equation \(\underset{\sim}{r_{2}}=(-t+1)\underset{\sim}{i}+(2t-2)\underset{\sim}{j}+(3t+6)\underset{\sim}{k}\) where \(t\in\mathbb R\). Find a vector parallel to \(l_{2}\).
questions.hint: Write \(\underset{\sim}{r_{2}}\) as (constant vector) \(+\ t\times\)(vector). The vector multiplying \(t\) is the DIRECTION of the line.

steps.explain: Separate the parts that contain \(t\) from the constants in each component.
The coefficient vector of \(t\) is the direction of \(l_{2}\).
Why not the others: B is the constant part, i.e. the position vector of the point at \(t=0\) (a point, not the direction); C and D have a wrong sign on one component.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Direction = the vector multiplying \(t\).

questions.stem: \(l_{1}\) has equation \(\underset{\sim}{r_{1}}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 2\\-3\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\ 2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(l_{2}\) has equation \(\underset{\sim}{r_{2}}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\ 6\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 2\\ 3\end{pmatrix}\). Find the point of intersection of \(l_{1}\) and \(l_{2}\).
questions.hint: At an intersection point the \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) coordinates of \(\underset{\sim}{r_{1}}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{r_{2}}\) are equal. Solve two of the three equations for \(s\) and \(t\), then CHECK in the third.

steps.explain: Equate the \(x\)-, \(y\)- and \(z\)-components (use different letters \(s\) and \(t\) for the two lines).
Tidy (1) and (2): (1) gives \(s+t=2\); (2) gives \(4=2s+2t\), i.e. \(s+t=2\) again — so these two are the same. Use (1) and (3) instead. From (3): \(2s-3t=9\).
Eliminate \(s\): (3) \(-\) 2\(\times\)(1) gives \(-5t=5\).
Check in equation (2): LHS \(2-2(3)=-4\); RHS \(-2+2(-1)=-4\) ✓. All three equations hold, so the lines DO intersect.
Substitute \(s=3\) into \(\underset{\sim}{r_{1}}\) (or \(t=-1\) into \(\underset{\sim}{r_{2}}\): both give the same point).
Why not the others: B and C have an arithmetic slip in the \(z\)- or \(x\)-component; D is false because the check in the third equation works.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Equate components; solve; check the third equation.

questions.stem: Show that the lines \(\underset{\sim}{r}=(1,7,5)+\lambda(1,-2,2)\) and \(\underset{\sim}{r}=(2,1,3)+\mu(0,1,1)\) are perpendicular.
questions.answer: The direction vectors are (1, −2, 2) and (0, 1, 1). Their dot product is 1·0 + (−2)(1) + 2·1 = 0 − 2 + 2 = 0, so the lines are perpendicular.
questions.hint: Two lines are perpendicular when the dot product of their direction vectors is zero.

steps.explain: Direction vectors: \(\underset{\sim}{d_1}=(1,-2,2)\) and \(\underset{\sim}{d_2}=(0,1,1)\).
Dot product.
The dot product is zero, so the lines are perpendicular. ✓

questions.stem: With respect to a fixed origin \(O\), the lines \(l_{1}\) and \(l_{2}\) are given by \(l_{1}:\ \mathbf{r}=9\mathbf{i}+13\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k}+\lambda(\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k})\) and \(l_{2}:\ \mathbf{r}=2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}+\mu(2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})\), where \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) are scalar parameters. Given that the point \(A\) has position vector \(4\mathbf{i}+16\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k}\) and that the point \(P(x_{1},y_{1},z_{1})\) lies on \(l_{1}\) such that \(AP\) is perpendicular to \(l_{1}\), find the exact coordinates of \(P\).
questions.hint: \(P\) is on \(l_{1}\), so \(P=(9+\lambda,\ 13+4\lambda,\ -3-2\lambda)\) for some \(\lambda\). Find \(\overrightarrow{AP}=\overrightarrow{OP}-\overrightarrow{OA}\), then use \(\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\underset{\sim}{d}=0\) where \(\underset{\sim}{d}\) is the direction vector of \(l_{1}\).

steps.explain: A general point of \(l_{1}\).
Vector \(\overrightarrow{AP}=\overrightarrow{OP}-\overrightarrow{OA}\) with \(A=(4,16,-3)\).
\(AP\perp l_{1}\) means \(\overrightarrow{AP}\) is perpendicular to the direction vector \((1,4,-2)\): their dot product is 0.
Expand and collect \(\lambda\)-terms and constants.
Solve for \(\lambda\).
Substitute \(\lambda=\dfrac{1}{3}\) into the point of \(l_{1}\).
Why not the others: \((10,17,-5)\) is the point with \(\lambda=1\); \((6,1,3)\) is the intersection with \(l_{2}\) (\(\lambda=-3\)); the last option uses a wrong \(\lambda\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: P on l1: write it with λ, then AP · d = 0.

questions.stem: Consider the line \(\underset{\sim}{r}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\ 3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-5\\ 3\end{pmatrix}\) where \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\). Show that the line through the points \(A(2,3)\) and \(B(-1,-2)\) is perpendicular to \(\underset{\sim}{r}\).

steps.explain: Direction of \(\underset{\sim}{r}\): \(\underset{\sim}{d}=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\ 3\end{pmatrix}\).
Dot product: multiply matching components and add: \((-3)(-5)+(-5)(3)=15-15\).

\(\underset{\sim}{u}\cdot\underset{\sim}{v}=|\underset{\sim}{u}||\underset{\sim}{v}|\cos\theta=0\) with both vectors non-zero means \(\cos\theta=0\), so \(\theta=90^{\circ}\): the lines are perpendicular. ∎
Why not the others: B uses \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\ 3\end{pmatrix}\) (the POINT vector) instead of the direction; C uses \(A+B\) not \(B-A\); D only shows the two directions are not parallel.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Perpendicular \(\Leftrightarrow\) dot product of directions \(=0\).

questions.stem: Which vector is perpendicular to \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\ 4\end{pmatrix}\)?
questions.hint: Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product is ZERO. Multiply matching components, add, and test each option.

steps.explain: Test A: \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\-4\\ 8\end{pmatrix}\) is just \(2\times\) the given vector (PARALLEL), so the dot product is positive.
Test B: it is \(-1\times\) the given vector (parallel again).
Test C.
Test D.
The dot product is 0 only for D, so D is perpendicular.
So the correct choice is option D.

keyPoints.note: Perpendicular \(\iff\) dot product \(=0\).

questions.stem: For \(Q=(2,-3,4)\), \(R=(-7,1,0)\), find the plane of points \(P=(x,y,z)\) equidistant from Q and R.
questions.hint: Set \(|P-Q|^2=|P-R|^2\). Expand and cancel the matching \(x^2+y^2+z^2\) terms.

steps.explain:
Set up the algebraic condition for all points (P(x, y, z)) equidistant from (Q(2, -3, 4)) and (R(-7, 1, 0)).
By definition, (|PQ| = |PR|), which is equivalent to equating the squared 3D Euclidean distances (|PQ|^2 = |PR|^2).
- (|PQ|^2 = (x - 2)^2 + (y - (-3))^2 + (z - 4)^2 = (x - 2)^2 + (y + 3)^2 + (z - 4)^2
- (|PR|^2 = (x - (-7))^2 + (y - 1)^2 + (z - 0)^2 = (x + 7)^2 + (y - 1)^2 + z^2

steps.explain:
Expand both sides of the equation and cancel the matching quadratic terms (x^2 + y^2 + z^2).
- Left side: ((x^2 - 4x + 4) + (y^2 + 6y + 9) + (z^2 - 8z + 16) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 4x + 6y - 8z + 29
- Right side: ((x^2 + 14x + 49) + (y^2 - 2y + 1) + z^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + 14x - 2y + 50
Subtracting (x^2 + y^2 + z^2) from both sides leaves a linear equation in (x, y, z), showing that the locus is indeed a flat plane passing through the midpoint (Mleft(-\frac{5}{2}, -1, 2\right)).

steps.explain:
Collect all variables on one side and constants on the other side to obtain the standard plane equation.
7104-4x + 6y - 8z + 29 = 14x - 2y + 50 \implies 29 - 50 = (14 + 4)x + (-2 - 6)y + 8z \implies 18x - 8y + 8z = -217104
**Geometric Verification:**
- The segment vector is \(\vec{QR} = R - Q = (-7 - 2, 1 - (-3), 0 - 4) = (-9, 4, -4)\).
- The normal vector to the perpendicular bisector plane is parallel to \(\vec{QR}\): \(\vec{n} = -2\vec{QR} = (18, -8, 8)\).
- The plane passes through midpoint \(M = \left(-\frac{5}{2}, -1, 2\right)\): \(18\left(-\frac{5}{2}\right) - 8(-1) + 8(2) = -45 + 8 + 16 = -21\).
This confirms the exact equation of the plane.

steps.explain: This is a quadratic in \(\lambda\). One point of intersection means exactly one solution, i.e. a repeated root, so \(\lambda=-\frac{B}{2A}\).

parts.answer: Intersection: \(|\mathbf{a}+\lambda\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{c}|^2=r^2\), i.e. \(\lambda^2|\mathbf{b}|^2+2\lambda\,\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c})+|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c}|^2-r^2=0\). Only one intersection ⇒ this quadratic in λ has one (repeated) root, so λ = −B/(2A) = \(-\frac{2\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c})}{2|\mathbf{b}|^2}=\frac{\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})}{|\mathbf{b}|^2}\).

keyPoints.note: One intersection ⇒ the quadratic in λ has a repeated root λ = −B/(2A).

parts.stem: Hence, show that the tangent to the sphere is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
parts.hint: Dot the radius vector R(λ) − c with b and use λ from (i).

steps.explain: The radius to the point of contact is \(\overrightarrow{CF}=\mathbf R(\lambda)-\mathbf{c}\); the tangent has direction \(\mathbf{b}\).
Substitute \(\lambda\) from (i).
A zero dot product means the radius is perpendicular to the tangent.

meta.source: Barker 2025 4U Trials & Solutions

parts.answer: The radius vector is \(\mathbf R(\lambda)-\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{a}+\lambda\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{c}\). Its dot product with the direction \(\mathbf{b}\) is \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{b}+\lambda|\mathbf{b}|^2=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})=0\). So the radius is perpendicular to the tangent.

keyPoints.note: Compute (R(λ) − c) · b using λ = b·(c − a)/|b|².

steps.explain: Points on the sphere satisfy \(|\mathbf{r}|=a\), i.e. \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{r}=a^2\). Substitute the line.
Expand; \(\mathbf{m}\cdot\mathbf{m}=1\) because \(\mathbf{m}\) is a unit vector.

parts.stem: Prove that a tangent to the sphere will always be perpendicular to the sphere’s radius at the point of contact.
parts.hint: For a tangent the quadratic has a repeated root λ = −b·m; then check m·p = 0.

steps.explain: For a tangent there is exactly one intersection: \(\Delta=0\), so \(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{b}-a^2=(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{m})^2\). The quadratic from (i) becomes a perfect square.
The point of contact (which is also the radius vector, since the centre is \(O\)):
Dot with the tangent's direction \(\mathbf{m}\), using \(\mathbf{m}\cdot\mathbf{m}=1\).
So the radius is perpendicular to the tangent.

parts.answer: For a tangent Δ = 0, i.e. \(a^2=\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{b}-(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{m})^2\); the quadratic becomes \((\lambda+\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{m})^2=0\), so λ = −b·m. The contact point is \(\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{b}-(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{m})\mathbf{m}\). Then \(\mathbf{m}\cdot\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{m}\cdot\mathbf{b}-(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{m})(\mathbf{m}\cdot\mathbf{m})=0\). So the radius p is perpendicular to the tangent direction m.

questions.stem: Find the radius and centre of the sphere: \(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}+x-3y+2z+2=0\)
questions.hint: Complete the square separately in \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). The centre is \((-\dfrac{\text{coeff of }x}{2},\ldots)\): HALVE each linear coefficient and change its sign.

steps.explain: Group the \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) terms and move the constant to the right.

Complete the square: add \(\left(\dfrac{\text{coeff}}{2}\right)^{2}\) to each bracket (and to the right side). \(x\): \(\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{1}{4}\); \(y\): \(\left(\dfrac{-3}{2}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{9}{4}\); \(z\): \(\left(\dfrac{2}{2}\right)^{2}=1\).
Add the right-hand side: \(-2+\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{9}{4}+1=-1+\dfrac{10}{4}=\dfrac{3}{2}\).
Compare with \((x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}+(z-c)^{2}=r^{2}\): the centre is \((a,b,c)\) — the OPPOSITE signs of the numbers inside the brackets.
Radius: \(r^{2}=\dfrac{3}{2}\), so \(r=\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{\sqrt6}{2}\).
Why not the others: A has the wrong signs on the centre; B and D divide the coefficients by the wrong numbers instead of halving them, so the centre and radius are wrong.
So the correct choice is option C.

questions.stem: The spheres represented by \(\left|\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\\ z\end{pmatrix}\right|=r_{1}\) and \(\left|\begin{pmatrix}x-a\\ y-b\\ z-c\end{pmatrix}\right|=r_{2}\), where \(r_{1},r_{2}\) are prime numbers, intersect at one point only. Let \(d=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}\). Which statement could be true?
questions.hint: Sphere 1 has centre \(O\) and radius \(r_{1}\); sphere 2 has centre \((a,b,c)\) and radius \(r_{2}\); \(d\) is the distance between the centres. Two spheres meet at ONE point only when they TOUCH — externally (\(d=r_{1}+r_{2}\)) or internally (\(d=|r_{1}-r_{2}|\)).

steps.explain: Read the equations: \(|\underset{\sim}{r}-\underset{\sim}{c}|=r\) is a sphere with centre \(\underset{\sim}{c}\). Centres \(O(0,0,0)\) and \((a,b,c)\); distance between centres \(d=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}\).
Touching externally: \(d=r_{1}+r_{2}\). Touching internally (one inside the other): \(d=r_{1}-r_{2}\) or \(d=r_{2}-r_{1}\).
A: \(r_{1}+r_{2}+d=0\) is impossible: all three are positive, so the sum is positive.
B: \(r_{1}-r_{2}=d\) matches internal touching, so it could be true. Example: \(r_{1}=7\), \(r_{2}=2\) (both prime) and centres \(5\) apart: \(7-2=5=d\) ✓.

D: external touching would need \(r_{1}r_{2}=r_{1}+r_{2}\), i.e. \(r_{1}=\dfrac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}+1\). For two DIFFERENT primes \(\dfrac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}\) is not an integer, a contradiction; internal touching \(r_{1}r_{2}=r_{1}-r_{2}\) is impossible too. So D is rejected (the paper takes \(r_{1}\ne r_{2}\); note that equal radii \(2\) and \(2\) would make D work, which the marking guide does not consider). Only B is the intended answer.
So the correct choice is option B.

keyPoints.note: One common point = tangent spheres: \(d=r_{1}+r_{2}\) or \(d=|r_{1}-r_{2}|\).

steps.explain: Complete the square: add \(\left(\dfrac{\text{coeff}}{2}\right)^{2}\) to both sides for each variable: \(x\): \(16\); \(y\): \(4\); \(z\): \(1\).
Write each as a square.
Compare with \((x-4)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}+(z-(-1))^{2}\): \(y+2=y-b\Rightarrow b=-2\). (Centre \((4,-2,-1)\), radius 5; the given \(x\)- and \(z\)-coordinates \(4\) and \(-1\) agree ✓.)
Why not the others: \(b=2\) forgets the sign change; \(-4\) halves wrongly (uses the coefficient \(4\) as the centre); \(-8\) comes from the \(x\)-term.
So the correct choice is option C.

keyPoints.note: Complete the square; \(y+2=y-b\).

questions.stem: Find the point(s) of intersection of the line with parametric equation \(\underset{\sim}{r}=\underset{\sim}{i}+3\underset{\sim}{j}-4\underset{\sim}{k}+t\left(\underset{\sim}{i}+2\underset{\sim}{j}+2\underset{\sim}{k}\right)\) and the sphere with equation \((x-1)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}+(z+4)^{2}=81\).
questions.hint: Write the line in coordinates \(x=\dots,\ y=\dots,\ z=\dots\) (all in terms of \(t\)), substitute into the sphere’s equation, solve for \(t\), then put each \(t\) back into the line.

steps.explain: Read off the parametric equations from the vector equation.
Substitute into \((x-1)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}+(z+4)^{2}=81\): each bracket simplifies nicely.
Simplify and solve: two values of \(t\) means two intersection points.
\(t=3\): substitute into the parametric equations.
Check one point: \((4-1)^{2}+(9-3)^{2}+(2+4)^{2}=9+36+36=81\) ✓. (The line passes through the CENTRE \((1,3,-4)\), so the two points are \(\pm3\) direction-lengths of 3, i.e. 9 away.)
Why not the others: B drops \(t=-3\) (a square equation has two roots); C uses \(t=\pm9\) (forgot to take the square root of \(t^{2}=9\) properly: \(t=\pm3\)); D uses \(t=\pm1\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Substitute \(x,y,z\) in terms of \(t\) into the sphere.

questions.stem:
A particle moves along a curve so that its position at time \(t\) is given by \(\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix}2t\\ t^2\\ t^3\end{pmatrix}\).

The acceleration at \(t=1\) is:
questions.hint: Differentiate each component twice, then substitute t = 1.

steps.explain: Differentiate each component to get the velocity.
Differentiate again for the acceleration.
The \(\mathbf{i}\) component is 0, because \(2t\) differentiated twice is 0.

meta.source: Barker 2025 4U Trials & Solutions

keyPoints.note: Acceleration is the second derivative of each component.

questions.stem:
Three different particles move in the \(xy\)-plane according to trajectories defined parametrically by:
\(\mathbf{R}_1(t)=\cos(t)\mathbf{i}+\sin(t)\mathbf{j}\)
\(\mathbf{R}_2(t)=\cos(2t)\mathbf{i}+\sin(2t)\mathbf{j}\)
\(\mathbf{R}_3(t)=\sin(t)\mathbf{i}+\cos(t)\mathbf{j}\)

For each particle, describe:
1. the shape of the path
2. the period of the motion
3. the direction of the motion
questions.hint: Check x² + y², the time to repeat, and where each particle goes from t = 0.

steps.explain: Shape: each has \(x^2+y^2=1\) (e.g. \(\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1\)), so all three paths are the unit circle.
Period: \(\mathbf R_1\) and \(\mathbf R_3\) repeat when \(t\) increases by \(2\pi\); \(\mathbf R_2\) uses \(2t\), so it repeats twice as fast.

Direction: track the start and a quarter-period later. \(\mathbf R_1\): \((1,0)\to(0,1)\) — anticlockwise. \(\mathbf R_2\): \((1,0)\to(0,1)\) at \(t=\frac\pi4\) — anticlockwise. \(\mathbf R_3\): \((0,1)\to(1,0)\) — clockwise.

questions.stem:
Let \(\mathbf{r}(t)=\left(1-\sqrt{a}\cos t\right)\mathbf{i}+\left(1-\frac1b\sin t\right)\mathbf{j}\) for \(t\ge0\) and \(a,b\in R^+\) be the path of a particle moving in the Cartesian plane.

The path of the particle will always be a circle if
questions.hint: Eliminate t with cos²t + sin²t = 1, then make the two coefficients equal.

steps.explain: Write the two components and make \(\cos t\) and \(\sin t\) the subjects.
steps.work: \(x=1-\sqrt{a}\cos t\Rightarrow\cos t=\frac{1-x}{\sqrt a},\qquad y=1-\frac1b\sin t\Rightarrow\sin t=b(1-y)\)

steps.explain: Use \(\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1\).
This is a circle (centre \((1,1)\)) only when the coefficients of the two squares are equal.
Then the radius is \(\sqrt a\). Otherwise the path is an ellipse.

keyPoints.note: Eliminate t; a circle needs equal coefficients on (x − 1)² and (y − 1)².

questions.stem: Consider the following parametric curve given by \(\underset{\sim}{r} = \begin{pmatrix}\cos t\\\ sin t\\ t\end{pmatrix}\) from \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\). Which of the following best represents the \(xz\) projection of \(\underset{\sim}{r}\)?
options: The curve \(x=\cos z\), for \(0\le z\le 2\pi\), starting at \((1,0)\)
The curve \(z=\sin x\), starting at the origin
questions.hint: The xz projection drops the y-coordinate. So keep \(x = \cos t\) and \(z = t\), and eliminate t.

steps.explain: The three components are \(x = \cos t\), \(y = \sin t\), \(z = t\). The projection onto the xz plane keeps x and z and drops y.
Substitute \(t = z\) into the x equation to get a relation between x and z.
Describe the curve: at \(z=0\) it is at \(x=1\). As z increases the curve moves left to \(x=-1\) at \(z=\pi\) and back to \(x=1\) at \(z=2\pi\). The z-axis is vertical in the picture.
steps.work: Starts at (1, 0), a wave in x against z.

steps.explain: Check the options: A is a circle (not a projection of this curve). B and D are graphs of z against x, which is the wrong way round. Only C matches \(x = \cos z\).

keyPoints.note: Keep x and z; drop y.

questions.stem: A vector equation is given by \(\underset{\sim}{v}=\underset{\sim}{c}+\underset{\sim}{a}\cos t+\underset{\sim}{b}\sin t\) where \(\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ -2\end{pmatrix},\ \underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\ -2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{c}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\ -2\end{pmatrix}\). Find the Cartesian equation of the vector equation and describe it geometrically.
options: The circle \((x-3)^2+(y+2)^2=8\), centre \((3,-2)\) and radius \(2\sqrt{2}\), traversed clockwise
The circle \((x-3)^2+(y+2)^2=8\), centre \((3,-2)\) and radius \(2\sqrt{2}\), traversed anticlockwise
The circle \((x-3)^2+(y+2)^2=64\), centre \((3,-2)\) and radius 8, traversed clockwise
questions.hint: Write the components: \(x=3+2\cos t-2\sin t\) and \(y=-2-2\cos t-2\sin t\). Square \(x-3\) and \(y+2\) and add.

steps.explain: Components.
Square and add.
Geometric description: a circle with centre \((3,-2)\) and radius \(\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}\).

Direction: at \(t=0\) the point is \((5,-4)\) and the velocity is \(\dfrac{d}{dt}(x,y)=(-2\sin t-2\cos t,\ 2\sin t-2\cos t)=(-2,-2)\): the point moves down and left from the lower-right of the circle, i.e. CLOCKWISE → A

keyPoints.note: Eliminate t using cos² + sin² = 1.

questions.stem: Which vector equation best describes the curve below?
questions.hint: Split the curve into its horizontal motion (the \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) terms make a circle of radius 1) and its height \(z(t)\). Compare how the HEIGHT grows with the picture: many tight loops near the bottom, then a very fast rise.

steps.explain: Horizontal motion: all four options have \(x,y\) given by \(\sin t,\cos t\) (or \(\cos t,\sin t\)), so the curve winds around the \(z\)-axis in a circle of radius 1. This does not separate the options.

Height: the picture shows MANY loops squeezed together near the base \(z\approx0\), then the curve shoots up very steeply. So \(z\) must be very small for many turns of \(t\) and then grow explosively.
steps.work: \(z\to0\text{ slowly as }t\to-\infty,\quad z\text{ explodes as }t\text{ increases}\)

steps.explain: Test \(z=2^{t}\): for negative \(t\), \(2^{t}\) is tiny (\(2^{-5}=0.03\)) so the curve hugs the base, then \(2^{t}\) doubles every \(2\pi\)... faster and faster: \(z=1,2,4,8,\dots\) (red points).

Rule out the others: \(z=t\) (C) rises at a constant pitch (evenly spaced coils); \(z=t^{2}\) (A) is symmetric about \(t=0\) and has widely spaced loops straight away; \(z=\ln t\) (B) exists only for \(t>0\), goes to \(-\infty\) at \(t\to0\) and rises more and more slowly.
So the correct choice is option D.

keyPoints.note: Circle in the xy-plane plus a height that stays tiny for many turns then grows explosively.

questions.stem: A spiral starts at the origin and completes two clockwise spirals to end at \((0,2\pi)\). Its position from \(t=0\) to \(t=T\) is shown in the diagram. The parametric equations of the spiral are \(x=f(t)\), \(y=g(t)\) for \([0,T]\). Find \(f(t)\), \(g(t)\) and \(T\).
questions.hint: A spiral has the form \((x,y)=(kt\cos t,\ kt\sin t)\) (ANTICLOCKWISE from the \(x\)-axis). To go CLOCKWISE starting upward on the \(y\)-axis swap them: \((kt\sin t,\ kt\cos t)\). Use the end point \((0,2\pi)\) to find \(k\) and \(T\).

steps.explain: At \(t=0\) the spiral is at the origin and the distance from the origin grows steadily: radius \(r=kt\). The radius increases with \(t\), so \(x\) and \(y\) both carry the factor \(kt\).

Direction: the spiral first moves from the origin to the RIGHT (the point \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) on the positive \(x\)-axis), then down, then left, then up: CLOCKWISE. Clockwise motion starting at angle \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (the \(+y\) direction) uses \(x=r\sin t\), \(y=r\cos t\).

Two complete clockwise turns means the angle \(t\) goes through \(2\times2\pi=4\pi\), so the spiral ends at \(t=T=4\pi\). There \(\sin4\pi=0\) and \(\cos4\pi=1\), so the end point is \((0,\ k\cdot4\pi)\).
The end point is \((0,2\pi)\): \(4\pi k=2\pi\), so \(k=\dfrac{1}{2}\).

Check against the diagram: at \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\): \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{4}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},0\right)\) ✓ (the label \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) on the \(x\)-axis). At \(t=\pi\): \(\left(0,-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\) ✓. At \(t=2\pi\): \((0,\pi)\) ✓.
Why not the others: B swaps sine and cosine (anticlockwise, and it would start along the \(x\)-axis); C and D have \(T=2\pi\) (one turn only) and/or \(k=1\) (which would end at \((0,4\pi)\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Clockwise: \(x=r\sin t\), \(y=r\cos t\); \(r=kt\); end \((0,2\pi)\).

questions.stem: The parametric equations of a second spiral are \(x=g(t)\), \(y=f(t)\) for \(\left[0,\dfrac{T}{2}\right]\), where \(f(t)=\dfrac{t}{2}\sin t\), \(g(t)=\dfrac{t}{2}\cos t\) and \(T=4\pi\) describe the first spiral. If the second spiral was drawn on the axes above, how many points of intersection would it have with the first spiral?
questions.hint: The second spiral is \(x=\dfrac{t}{2}\cos t\), \(y=\dfrac{t}{2}\sin t\) for \(0\le t\le2\pi\) (anticlockwise, half the length). Both spirals have distance \(\dfrac{t}{2}\) from the origin at parameter \(t\), so a common point must have the SAME parameter value.

steps.explain: Second spiral: swap \(f\) and \(g\), and \(\dfrac{T}{2}=2\pi\).

On each spiral the distance from the origin is \(\dfrac{t}{2}\) (since \(\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{t}{2}\sin t\right)^{2}+\left(\dfrac{t}{2}\cos t\right)^{2}}=\dfrac{t}{2}\)). So a common point needs the same radius, i.e. the SAME \(t\) (the radius determines the parameter).
Same \(t\): the points coincide when \(\dfrac{t}{2}\sin t=\dfrac{t}{2}\cos t\) (and the \(y\)'s match too, which is the same equation). So \(t(\sin t-\cos t)=0\).
\(t=0\): both start at the origin. \(\tan t=1\) on \([0,2\pi]\): \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) and \(t=\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\).

That is 3 intersection points (the origin and the two red points, which lie on the line \(y=x\)). Why not the others: counting only the two non-origin points gives 2; 1 or 4 misses/invents intersections.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: how many points of intersection would it have with the first spiral?
keyPoints.note: Same radius \(\dfrac{t}{2}\) \(\Rightarrow\) same \(t\); \(\sin t=\cos t\).

questions.stem: In a regular tetrahedron with all edge lengths 1, \(BX:XC=AY:YB=x:(1-x)\). Find \(|OY|\).

parts.stem: Determine, in component form, the vectors \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AC}\).
parts.hint: AB = OB − OA (end minus start).

steps.explain: A vector from \(A\) to \(B\) is "end minus start".
Subtract component by component.
Do the same for \(\overrightarrow{AC}\).
Subtracting the other way round (\(\overrightarrow{OA}-\overrightarrow{OB}\)) gives \(\overrightarrow{BA}\) — every sign is reversed.

questions.stem:
The diagram shows a rhombus.
Adjacent sides are represented by the two vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\).

It follows that:

questions.hint: Use |a| = |b| and expand the dot product of the two diagonals.

steps.explain: In a rhombus all sides are equal, so \(|\mathbf{a}|=|\mathbf{b}|\). But the sides are not perpendicular in general (that would be a square), and \(\mathbf{a}\neq\mathbf{b}\) because they point in different directions. So A and B are not true in general.
The diagonals of the parallelogram formed by \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) are \(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\).

steps.explain: Expand their dot product, using \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}=|\mathbf{a}|^2\).

So the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular, which is option C. Option D, \(|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}|=|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|\) (equal diagonals), holds only when \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\), i.e. for a rectangle or square.

steps.explain: Projecting onto the xy plane keeps x and y and sets z to 0. So the projection of \((2,3,1)\) is \(\underset{\sim}{u}=(2,3,0)\).
Find the length: \(|\underset{\sim}{u}|=\sqrt{2^2+3^2+0^2}=\sqrt{13}\).
Divide by the length to make a unit vector: \(\hat u=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}}(2,3,0)\).

questions.stem: A unit vector perpendicular to \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\ 1\\ -2\end{pmatrix}\) is
questions.hint: Two conditions: (1) PERPENDICULAR means dot product \(=0\). (2) UNIT vector means length \(=1\). Check both conditions for each option.

steps.explain: Options A and C are multiples of \(\left(5,1,-2\right)\) itself, so they are PARALLEL to the given vector, not perpendicular. Check the dot product: \(5\cdot5+1\cdot1+(-2)(-2)=30\ne0\).
Options B and D point along \((2,-4,3)\). Test perpendicularity with the dot product.
Now the length of \((2,-4,3)\).
A unit vector is the vector divided by its LENGTH, so we need \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{29}}\), not \(\dfrac{1}{29}\). In B the length is \(\dfrac{\sqrt{29}}{29}\ne1\).
Only D is both perpendicular and of length 1.
So the correct choice is option D.

keyPoints.note: Perpendicular: dot = 0. Unit: divide by the length.

questions.stem: Let \(\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ -1\\ -2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{v}=\begin{pmatrix}a\\ 2\\ -1\end{pmatrix}\). Given that the vector projection of \(\underset{\sim}{v}\) in the direction of \(\underset{\sim}{u}\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{4}{9}\\ -\dfrac{2}{9}\\ -\dfrac{4}{9}\end{pmatrix}\), find the value of \(a\).
questions.hint: Vector projection of \(\underset{\sim}{v}\) onto \(\underset{\sim}{u}\) \(=\dfrac{\underset{\sim}{v}\cdot\underset{\sim}{u}}{|\underset{\sim}{u}|^{2}}\,\underset{\sim}{u}\). Compute the dot product (it contains \(a\)) and \(|\underset{\sim}{u}|^{2}\), then match one component.

steps.explain: Dot product \(\underset{\sim}{v}\cdot\underset{\sim}{u}\).
Length squared of \(\underset{\sim}{u}\).
Vector projection \(=\dfrac{\underset{\sim}{v}\cdot\underset{\sim}{u}}{|\underset{\sim}{u}|^{2}}\underset{\sim}{u}=\dfrac{2a}{9}\underset{\sim}{u}\).
Match with the given projection: compare the first components (all three give the same equation).

Check the second: \(-\dfrac{2a}{9}=-\dfrac{2}{9}\) ✓. Why not the others: \(a=2\) would give \(\dfrac{8}{9}\) in the first component; \(a=-1\) the wrong sign; \(a=\dfrac{3}{2}\) gives \(\dfrac{2}{3}\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Projection = (v·u ÷ |u|²) u.

questions.stem: By considering the scalar product \(\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}\) where \(\underset{\sim}{a}=a_{1}\underset{\sim}{i}+a_{2}\underset{\sim}{j}+a_{3}\underset{\sim}{k}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{b}=b_{1}\underset{\sim}{i}+b_{2}\underset{\sim}{j}+b_{3}\underset{\sim}{k}\), prove that \(\left(a_{1}b_{1}+a_{2}b_{2}+a_{3}b_{3}\right)^{2}\le\left(a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+a_{3}^{2}\right)\left(b_{1}^{2}+b_{2}^{2}+b_{3}^{2}\right)\)
questions.hint: Write \(\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}\) in TWO ways: components \(a_{1}b_{1}+a_{2}b_{2}+a_{3}b_{3}\) and geometrically \(|\underset{\sim}{a}||\underset{\sim}{b}|\cos\theta\). Square it and use \(\cos^{2}\theta\le1\).

steps.explain: Component form of the dot product (multiply matching components and add).
Geometric form, where \(\theta\) is the angle between the vectors.
Square both sides.
For every real \(\theta\), \(0\le\cos^{2}\theta\le1\), so the right-hand side is at most \(|\underset{\sim}{a}|^{2}|\underset{\sim}{b}|^{2}\) (multiplying by a non-negative number keeps \(\le\)).

Why not the others: B reverses the inequality (\(\cos^{2}\theta\le1\), not \(\ge1\)); C uses \(\sin\theta\) (the dot product has \(\cos\theta\)); D forgets to square the magnitudes (and \(|\underset{\sim}{a}|\) is a square ROOT, not the sum of squares).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}=|\underset{\sim}{a}||\underset{\sim}{b}|\cos\theta\) and \(\cos^{2}\theta\le1\).

steps.explain: Expand the dot product like brackets (the dot product is distributive and commutative).
Substitute \(\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{a}=\underset{\sim}{b}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}=1\): the \(m\) and \(-m\) cancel.
Set equal to 1 and use \(\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}=\dfrac{1}{2}\).
Square root: BOTH signs.
Check \(m=-\sqrt3\): \(m^{2}-1=2\) as well ✓. Why not the others: B drops the negative root; C solves \(m^{2}-1=1\) (forgot to multiply by 2); D solves \(m^{2}-1=3\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{a}=1\); \(\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}=\dfrac{1}{2}\); \((m^{2}-1)\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}=1\).

questions.stem: Given \(\underset{\sim}{a}=\underset{\sim}{i}-\underset{\sim}{j}+2\underset{\sim}{k}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{b}=3\underset{\sim}{i}-2\underset{\sim}{j}+\underset{\sim}{k}\), the projection of \(\underset{\sim}{a}\) onto \(\underset{\sim}{b}\) is:
questions.hint: Projection of \(\underset{\sim}{a}\) ONTO \(\underset{\sim}{b}\): \(\operatorname{proj}_{b}a=\dfrac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}\,\underset{\sim}{b}\) — the answer is a multiple of \(\underset{\sim}{b}\) (the vector you project ONTO).

steps.explain: Scalar multiple of \(b\).
Why not the others: B uses the wrong denominator (6); C, D are multiples of \(a\) (they project onto the wrong vector).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(\dfrac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}\,b\)

questions.stem: Find the angle between the vectors \(\underset{\sim}{u}=(3,5,-2)\) and \(\underset{\sim}{v}=(-1,2,3)\).
questions.hint: The angle between two vectors: \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{u\cdot v}{|u||v|}\). Work out the DOT product first, then both LENGTHS (square root of the sum of squares).

steps.explain: Dot product: multiply matching components and add.
Lengths.
Substitute: \(\sqrt{38}\sqrt{14}=\sqrt{532}\).
\(\theta=\cos^{-1}(0.0434)\approx87.5^{\circ}=1.527\) radians (almost perpendicular, because the dot product is small).
Why not the others: B uses \(|u||v|=14\); C uses a dot product of 13; D would need the vectors to point in opposite directions.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{u\cdot v}{|u||v|}\)

questions.stem: If \(\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-2\\ 4\end{pmatrix}\) is a non zero vector, then the corresponding unit vector is:
questions.hint: A unit vector has length 1. Divide EVERY component of \(\underset{\sim}{u}\) by its magnitude \(|\underset{\sim}{u}|\).

steps.explain: Magnitude: square each component, add, then square root.
Divide each component by 6 and simplify.
Check the length is 1: \(\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{2}+\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{2}+\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{4}{9}+\dfrac{1}{9}+\dfrac{4}{9}=1\) ✓.
Why not the others: A divided by 6 twice (by 24); C divided by 4 and D by 2, so their lengths are \(\dfrac{3}{2}\) and \(\sqrt6\), not 1.
So the correct choice is option B.

keyPoints.note: \(\hat u=\dfrac{u}{|u|}\); check the length is 1.

questions.stem: The line \(l_{1}\) has direction \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\ 2\end{pmatrix}\) and the line \(l_{2}\) has direction \(\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 2\\ 3\end{pmatrix}\). Find the acute angle between \(l_{1}\) and \(l_{2}\). Give your answer in degrees correct to one decimal place.
questions.hint: The angle between lines is the angle between their direction vectors: \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}}{|\underset{\sim}{a}||\underset{\sim}{b}|}\). Make sure the final angle is ACUTE.

steps.explain: Dot product: multiply matching components and add.
Magnitudes.
Substitute into the formula.
Inverse cosine (calculator in DEGREE mode).
The dot product is positive, so \(\theta\) is already acute.
Why not the others: B is \(180^{\circ}-84.9^{\circ}\) (obtuse); C is \(90^{\circ}-84.9^{\circ}\); D is from using \(|\underset{\sim}{b}|=\sqrt{13}\) or a similar slip.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: The coordinates of three points are \(A=(1,0,5)\), \(B=(-1,2,4)\) and \(C=(3,5,2)\). Prove that \(\angle ABC\) is a right angle. Which working is correct?
options: \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\ 2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\), \(\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 5\\-3\end{pmatrix}\); \(\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=-4+10+3=9\ne0\), so \(\angle ABC\) is not a right angle.

\(\overrightarrow{BA}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\ 1\end{pmatrix}\), \(\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\ 3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\); \(\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=8+6+2=16\ne0\), so \(\angle ABC\) is not a right angle.
questions.hint: The angle at \(B\) is between the vectors that START at \(B\): \(\overrightarrow{BA}\) and \(\overrightarrow{BC}\). Each vector is (end point) \(-\) (start point). If their dot product is 0, the angle is \(90^{\circ}\).

steps.explain: Find \(\overrightarrow{BA}=A-B\): subtract the coordinates of \(B\) from those of \(A\).
Find \(\overrightarrow{BC}=C-B\).
Dot product: multiply matching components and add.
Dot product \(=0\) and both vectors are non-zero, so they are perpendicular: \(\angle ABC=90^{\circ}\).

Why not the others: B uses the vectors at \(A\) (the angle at \(A\), not at \(B\)); C has a sign error in the dot product; D uses the vectors at \(C\), and a dot product of 29 would NOT mean \(90^{\circ}\) (it must be 0).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Prove that \(\angle ABC\) is a right angle
keyPoints.note: Vectors from \(B\): \(\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=0\).

questions.stem: The unit vector in the same direction as \(\underset{\sim}{u}=2\underset{\sim}{i}+2\underset{\sim}{j}-\underset{\sim}{k}\) is which of the following?
questions.hint: A unit vector in the same direction is \(\hat u=\dfrac{\underset{\sim}{u}}{|\underset{\sim}{u}|}\): divide every component by the magnitude (the length).

steps.explain: Write the components: \(\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\).
Magnitude: square, add, square root.
Divide by the magnitude.
Check the length: \(\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{2}+\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{2}+\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{2}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{9}{9}}=1\) ✓.

Why not the others: C and D divide by 5 and 6 (lengths \(\dfrac{3}{5}\) and \(\dfrac{1}{2}\), not 1); A has the right direction but its length is \(\dfrac{1}{6}\) (\(\dfrac{-1}{36}\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-2\\ 1\end{pmatrix}=\dfrac1{18}\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\)).
So the correct choice is option B.

questions.stem: The projection of \(\overrightarrow{OA}\) onto \(\overrightarrow{OB}\) for \(A(4,2,-3)\) and \(B(-1,1,1)\) is which of the following?
questions.hint: The projection of \(\underset{\sim}{a}\) onto \(\underset{\sim}{b}\) is a VECTOR IN THE DIRECTION OF \(\underset{\sim}{b}\): \(\text{proj}=\dfrac{\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}}{|\underset{\sim}{b}|^{2}}\underset{\sim}{b}\).

steps.explain: Position vectors: \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\ 2\\-3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}\).
Dot product.
Squared length of \(\underset{\sim}{b}\).
Scalar factor \(=\dfrac{-5}{3}\); multiply by \(\underset{\sim}{b}\).

Why not the others: B forgets the minus sign of the dot product (\(-5\)); C and D are multiples of \(\underset{\sim}{a}\) (the projection must be a multiple of \(\underset{\sim}{b}\), the vector being projected ONTO).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(\dfrac{a\cdot b}{|b|^2}\,b\): a multiple of \(b\).

questions.stem: In rhombus \(ABCD\), \(\overrightarrow{AB}=a\), \(\overrightarrow{BC}=b\). \(BE\) extends \(AB\) with \(AB:BE=4:3\), and \(F\) is the midpoint of \(CD\). Find \(\overrightarrow{FE}\).

questions.stem:
\(OABC\) is a parallelogram and the point \(M\) is the midpoint of \(AB\).
The point \(N\) lies on the diagonal \(AC\) so that \(AN:NC=1:2\).

Let \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a}\) and \(\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf{c}\).

parts.stem: Find simplified expressions, in terms of \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{c}\), for each of the vectors \(\overrightarrow{AC}\), \(\overrightarrow{AN}\), \(\overrightarrow{ON}\) and \(\overrightarrow{NM}\).
parts.hint: AC = c − a; N is ⅓ of the way from A to C; AB = OC = c.

steps.explain: \(\overrightarrow{AC}\) goes from \(A\) to \(C\): end minus start. Since \(AN:NC=1:2\), \(N\) is one third of the way from \(A\) to \(C\).

keyPoints.note: AN:NC = 1:2, so N is one third of the way from A to C, so AN = ⅓ AC = ⅓(c − a).

parts.stem: Deduce, showing your reasoning, that \(O\), \(N\) and \(M\) are collinear.
parts.hint: Show NM is a scalar multiple of ON and note they share the point N.

steps.explain: Compare the two vectors found in part (i).
Both vectors are scalar multiples of \(2\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{c}\), so they are parallel.
Parallel vectors that share a common point \(N\) must lie on the same line. Therefore \(O\), \(N\) and \(M\) are collinear (and \(ON:NM=2:1\)).

questions.answer: Let \(\overrightarrow{AM}=\mathbf{p}\) and \(\overrightarrow{MB}=\mathbf{q}\). Since M bisects AC and BD, \(\overrightarrow{MC}=\overrightarrow{AM}=\mathbf{p}\) and \(\overrightarrow{DM}=\overrightarrow{MB}=\mathbf{q}\). In \(\triangle AMB\): \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{AM}+\overrightarrow{MB}=\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{q}\). In \(\triangle DMC\): \(\overrightarrow{DC}=\overrightarrow{DM}+\overrightarrow{MC}=\mathbf{q}+\mathbf{p}\). Hence \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{DC}\).

keyPoints.note: Bisecting means AM = MC and DM = MB as vectors, i.e. both equal p and q respectively.

keyPoints.text: Show that \(\mathbf b\cdot(\mathbf c-\mathbf a)=0\) and \(\mathbf c\cdot(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=0\).
keyPoints.note: Use the perpendicular altitude facts in the diagram. Since O lies on BE and CF, the vectors from O to B and C point along those altitudes.

parts.answer: BE\perp AC and CF\perp AB. As O lies on both altitudes, \(\mathbf b\parallel BE\), \(\mathbf c\parallel CF\), \(\mathbf c-\mathbf a=\overrightarrow{AC}\), and \(\mathbf b-\mathbf a=\overrightarrow{AB}\). Thus both stated dot products are zero.

parts.stem: Hence show that \(AD\perp BC\).
parts.hint: Expand the two dot-product equalities from the preceding part. This gives equal dot products \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b\) and \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c\); compare the directions of AD and BC.
parts.solution: From the first two equalities, \(\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf b=\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf a\). Therefore \(\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf c-\mathbf b)=0\). Since AD is on the same line as OA, its direction is parallel to \(\mathbf a\), while \(\mathbf c-\mathbf b\) is the direction of BC. Hence \(AD\perp BC\).

steps.explain: Expand the first equality from the preceding part.
steps.work: \(\mathbf b\cdot(\mathbf c-\mathbf a)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf a.\)

steps.explain: Expand the second equality. By symmetry of the dot product, \(\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf b=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c\).
steps.work: \(\mathbf c\cdot(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf b=\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf a.\)

steps.explain: Combine the equalities to obtain \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c\). Hence a is perpendicular to the direction vector of BC. The diagram highlights AO (the direction of AD) and BC.
steps.work: \(\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf c-\mathbf b)=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=0.\)

parts.stem: What geometrical property of the triangle has been proved?
parts.hint: Use the construction: O is already the intersection of two altitudes. The previous part proves the third altitude passes through O as well.
parts.solution: The altitudes of a triangle are concurrent (at the orthocentre).

steps.explain: BE and CF are altitudes and meet at O, so O lies on both. The previous part proved that AD is perpendicular to BC.
The construction also gives A, O and D on one straight line. Since D lies on BC and AD is perpendicular to BC, AD is the altitude from A.
steps.work: \(A,O,D\text{ are collinear},\qquad D\in BC,\qquad AD\perp BC.\)

steps.explain: Thus the three altitudes meet at O. The point where all three altitudes of a triangle meet is called the orthocentre.
steps.work: The altitudes are concurrent; \(O\) is the orthocentre of \(\triangle ABC\).

questions.stem: The points \(A(-3,2,6)\), \(B(-1,-3,-5)\), \(C(7,-1,-4)\) and \(D(5,4,7)\) form the vertices of the quadrilateral \(ABCD\). Deduce that \(ABCD\) is a parallelogram by showing that \(\vec{AB}=\vec{DC}\) and \(\vec{AD}=\vec{BC}\).
questions.answer: AB = (2,-5,-11) and DC = (2,-5,-11), so AB = DC. AD = (8,2,1) and BC = (8,2,1), so AD = BC. Opposite sides are equal and parallel, so ABCD is a parallelogram.
questions.hint: Write each vector as (end point) − (start point). Compare the components.

steps.explain: Find \(\vec{AD}=D-A=(8,2,1)\) and \(\vec{BC}=C-B=(8,2,1)\). So \(\vec{AD}=\vec{BC}\).
Equal vectors mean equal length and parallel direction. Opposite sides are parallel and equal, so ABCD is a parallelogram.

questions.hint: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so \(X\) is the midpoint of AC (or BD).

Add the coordinates of A and C: \(A+C=(-3+7,\;2-1,\;6-4)=(4,\;1,\;2)\).
Check with BD: \(\dfrac12(B+D)=\dfrac12(4,1,2)=(2,0.5,1)\), the same point.

options: \(\overrightarrow{AE}=2\underset{\sim}{u}+\underset{\sim}{v}\), so \(\overrightarrow{AP}=k(2\underset{\sim}{u}+\underset{\sim}{v})\). \(\overrightarrow{DC}=\underset{\sim}{u}+2\underset{\sim}{v}\), \(\overrightarrow{DP}=\mu(\underset{\sim}{u}+2\underset{\sim}{v})\), so \(\overrightarrow{AP}=\underset{\sim}{u}+\mu(\underset{\sim}{u}+2\underset{\sim}{v})\). Equate: \(2k\underset{\sim}{u}+k\underset{\sim}{v}=(1+\mu)\underset{\sim}{u}+2\mu\underset{\sim}{v}\). As \(\underset{\sim}{u},\underset{\sim}{v}\) are not parallel: \(2k=1+\mu\) and \(k=2\mu\). So \(2k=1+\dfrac{k}{2}\Rightarrow k=\dfrac{2}{3}\).

\(\overrightarrow{AP}=k(2\underset{\sim}{u}+\underset{\sim}{v})=\underset{\sim}{u}+\mu(\underset{\sim}{u}+2\underset{\sim}{v})\), so \(2k=1+\mu\) and \(k=2\mu\); since \(0<k<1\), \(k=\dfrac{2}{3}\) follows from the fact that the medians meet at the centroid.

steps.explain: \(D\) bisects \(AB\) so \(\overrightarrow{AD}=\overrightarrow{DB}=\underset{\sim}{u}\); \(E\) bisects \(BC\) so \(\overrightarrow{EC}=\overrightarrow{BE}=\underset{\sim}{v}\). Then \(\overrightarrow{AE}=\overrightarrow{AD}+\overrightarrow{DB}+\overrightarrow{BE}\) (purple line) and \(\overrightarrow{DC}=\overrightarrow{DB}+\overrightarrow{BE}+\overrightarrow{EC}\) (orange line).

Second route: \(A\to D\to P\), where \(P\) lies on \(DC\), so \(\overrightarrow{DP}=\mu\overrightarrow{DC}\) for some \(\mu\).

Equate. Because \(\underset{\sim}{u}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{v}\) are NOT parallel (they are two sides of a triangle), the coefficients of \(\underset{\sim}{u}\) must match and the coefficients of \(\underset{\sim}{v}\) must match.
From (2), \(\mu=\dfrac{k}{2}\). Substitute in (1).
Why not the others: B mixes up \(\overrightarrow{AE}\) and \(\overrightarrow{DC}\); C has an arithmetic slip; D quotes the centroid result instead of proving it with vectors.
So the correct choice is option A.

options: \(\overrightarrow{AC}=2\underset{\sim}{u}+2\underset{\sim}{v}\), so \(\overrightarrow{AF}=\underset{\sim}{u}+\underset{\sim}{v}\). \(\overrightarrow{FP}=-(\underset{\sim}{u}+\underset{\sim}{v})+\dfrac{2}{3}(2\underset{\sim}{u}+\underset{\sim}{v})=\dfrac{1}{3}\underset{\sim}{u}-\dfrac{1}{3}\underset{\sim}{v}\) and \(\overrightarrow{FB}=-(\underset{\sim}{u}+\underset{\sim}{v})+2\underset{\sim}{u}=\underset{\sim}{u}-\underset{\sim}{v}=3\overrightarrow{FP}\). So \(FB\parallel FP\) and they share the point \(F\): \(B,F,P\) are collinear.

\(\overrightarrow{AF}=\underset{\sim}{u}+\underset{\sim}{v}\). \(\overrightarrow{FP}=\dfrac{1}{3}\underset{\sim}{u}-\dfrac{1}{3}\underset{\sim}{v}\) and \(\overrightarrow{FB}=\underset{\sim}{u}+\underset{\sim}{v}\). Since both are multiples of \(\underset{\sim}{u}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{v}\), the points are collinear.
\(\overrightarrow{FP}=\dfrac{1}{3}\underset{\sim}{u}-\dfrac{1}{3}\underset{\sim}{v}\) and \(\overrightarrow{FB}=\underset{\sim}{u}-\underset{\sim}{v}\). These are parallel, so \(BF\parallel AC\).
\(B,F,P\) are three points inside the triangle, and any three points in a plane are collinear if they lie on the medians.
questions.hint: To show three points are collinear, show two vectors between them are PARALLEL (one is a scalar multiple of the other) AND share a common point. Express \(\overrightarrow{FP}\) and \(\overrightarrow{FB}\) in terms of \(\underset{\sim}{u},\underset{\sim}{v}\).

steps.explain: \(F\) bisects \(AC\). First \(\overrightarrow{AC}=\overrightarrow{AD}+\overrightarrow{DB}+\overrightarrow{BE}+\overrightarrow{EC}\), then halve it.
\(\overrightarrow{FP}=\overrightarrow{FA}+\overrightarrow{AP}\) with \(\overrightarrow{FA}=-\overrightarrow{AF}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AP}=\dfrac{2}{3}\overrightarrow{AE}\) (from part (i)).
\(\overrightarrow{FB}=\overrightarrow{FA}+\overrightarrow{AB}\) with \(\overrightarrow{AB}=2\underset{\sim}{u}\).

Compare: \(\underset{\sim}{u}-\underset{\sim}{v}=3\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\underset{\sim}{u}-\dfrac{1}{3}\underset{\sim}{v}\right)\), i.e. \(\overrightarrow{FB}=3\overrightarrow{FP}\) (green line \(BF\) passes through \(P\)).

questions.stem: Using vectors, show that the lines connecting any point on the semicircle \(y=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\) to the points \((1,0)\) and \((-1,0)\) are perpendicular. Which argument is correct?
options: Let \(P(x,y)\) be on the semicircle. The vectors are \(\overrightarrow{AP}=\begin{pmatrix}x+1\\ y\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\overrightarrow{BP}=\begin{pmatrix}x-1\\ y\end{pmatrix}\). Dot product \(=(x+1)(x-1)+y^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}-1=0\) since \(x^{2}+y^{2}=1\). So they are perpendicular.

Let \(P(x,y)\) be on the semicircle. The vectors are \(\begin{pmatrix}x+1\\ y\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}x-1\\ y\end{pmatrix}\). Dot product \(=(x+1)(x-1)+y=x^{2}+y-1\), which is \(0\) on the circle. So they are perpendicular.

The position vector of \(P\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}\). Then \(\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}=x^{2}+y^{2}=1\ne0\), so the lines are perpendicular.
The distances \(PA\) and \(PB\) are equal, so the two lines are perpendicular.
questions.hint: Two lines are perpendicular when the DOT PRODUCT of their direction vectors is 0. Write \(P=(x,y)\) with \(x^{2}+y^{2}=1\) (it is on the unit semicircle). Find the vectors \(\overrightarrow{AP}\) and \(\overrightarrow{BP}\) where \(A=(-1,0)\), \(B=(1,0)\).

steps.explain: Vector from \(A\) to \(P\) (blue): subtract coordinates, \(P-A\).
Vector from \(B\) to \(P\) (red): \(P-B\).

questions.stem: Three points \(P\), \(Q\) and \(R\) have position vectors \(\underset{\sim}{p}\), \(\underset{\sim}{q}\) and \(k\left(2\underset{\sim}{p}+\underset{\sim}{q}\right)\) respectively, relative to a fixed origin \(O\). The points \(O\), \(P\) and \(Q\) are not collinear. Find the value of \(k\) if \(\overrightarrow{QR}\) is parallel to \(\underset{\sim}{p}\).
questions.hint: Find \(\overrightarrow{QR}=\overrightarrow{OR}-\overrightarrow{OQ}\) and collect terms in \(\underset{\sim}{p}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{q}\). Parallel to \(\underset{\sim}{p}\) means \(\overrightarrow{QR}=\lambda\underset{\sim}{p}\). Since \(O,P,Q\) are not collinear, \(\underset{\sim}{p}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{q}\) are NOT parallel, so their coefficients must match separately.

steps.explain: Vector from \(Q\) to \(R\): \(\overrightarrow{QR}=\overrightarrow{OR}-\overrightarrow{OQ}\).
Expand and collect \(\underset{\sim}{p}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{q}\) terms.
Parallel to \(\underset{\sim}{p}\): \(\overrightarrow{QR}=\lambda\underset{\sim}{p}\) for some non-zero real number \(\lambda\).

\(\underset{\sim}{p}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{q}\) are not parallel (since \(O,P,Q\) are not collinear), so the coefficients of \(\underset{\sim}{q}\) on both sides must be equal: left \(k-1\), right \(0\).

Then \(\lambda=2k=2\), non-zero ✓, so \(\overrightarrow{QR}=2\underset{\sim}{p}\). Why not the others: other values of \(k\) leave a non-zero multiple of \(\underset{\sim}{q}\), so \(\overrightarrow{QR}\) is not parallel to \(\underset{\sim}{p}\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Coefficient of q must be zero.

steps.explain: Vector \(\overrightarrow{MB}=\overrightarrow{MO}+\overrightarrow{OB}=-\dfrac{1}{5}\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}\) (end minus start).
\(|\overrightarrow{MP}|=\dfrac{1}{6}|\overrightarrow{MB}|\) and \(P\) is on \(MB\), so \(\overrightarrow{MP}=\dfrac{1}{6}\overrightarrow{MB}\).

Go from \(O\) to \(M\) then to \(P\): \(\overrightarrow{OP}=\overrightarrow{OM}+\overrightarrow{MP}\). Combine the \(\underset{\sim}{a}\) terms: \(\dfrac{1}{5}-\dfrac{1}{30}=\dfrac{6}{30}-\dfrac{1}{30}=\dfrac{5}{30}=\dfrac{1}{6}\).

In the parallelogram \(\overrightarrow{OC}=\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}\), so \(\overrightarrow{OP}=\dfrac{1}{6}\overrightarrow{OC}\): \(\overrightarrow{OP}\) is parallel to \(\overrightarrow{OC}\) and shares the point \(O\), so \(P\) lies on \(OC\) (red line). ∎

questions.stem: Let \(OACB\) be a parallelogram with \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\underset{\sim}{a}\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\underset{\sim}{b}\), \(P\) lying on the diagonal \(OC\) with \(\overrightarrow{OP}=\dfrac{1}{6}\overrightarrow{OC}\). State the ratio of lengths \(OP:PC\).
questions.hint: If \(OP\) is \(\dfrac{1}{6}\) of \(OC\), then \(PC\) is the REMAINING \(\dfrac{5}{6}\). Compare the two parts, not part to whole.

steps.explain: From part (i): \(\overrightarrow{OP}=\dfrac{1}{6}\overrightarrow{OC}\), so \(OP=\dfrac16OC\).
\(P\) is on \(OC\), so \(PC=OC-OP=OC-\dfrac16OC=\dfrac{5}{6}\,OC\).
Ratio of the two parts (multiply by 6 to clear the fractions).
Why not the others: B compares OP with the whole diagonal (\(1:6\)); C is upside down; D mistakes \(OC\) for 5 parts.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(OP=\dfrac16OC\Rightarrow PC=\dfrac56OC\).

questions.stem: \(M\) and \(P\) are two points with position vectors \(\overrightarrow{OM}=\underset{\sim}{m}\) and \(\overrightarrow{OP}=\underset{\sim}{p}\) respectively. \(N\) is the midpoint of \(MP\) and has position vector \(\overrightarrow{ON}=\underset{\sim}{n}\). \(PQ\) is perpendicular to \(MN\) and \(\overrightarrow{NQ}=\lambda\overrightarrow{ON}\), where \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\). Show that \(\lambda=\dfrac{\left|\underset{\sim}{m}\right|^{2}+\left|\underset{\sim}{n}\right|^{2}-2\underset{\sim}{m}\cdot\underset{\sim}{n}}{\left|\underset{\sim}{n}\right|^{2}-\underset{\sim}{m}\cdot\underset{\sim}{n}}\).
